statement: PROPOSAL: a record groups the open decisions of the plans of the draft by the part of the draft they concern and the kind of the decision, or the units that leave one critical semantic of one contract open, or the manual actions of the plans by kind, or the open statements of the plans about units they write no resource for by the reason of the statement. It is a view: nothing here changes the draft, target-plan.json, a gate, or any class, confidence or eligibility, and every critical semantic stays open in the assessment. A review of a plan-decision record acts on the execution plan only, by its effect: an answer whose option is what the draft already carries out (ACK_CURRENT_ARTIFACT) frees the steps that wait for the decision; an option that changes the draft (REGENERATE_REQUIRED) or a redesign keeps them held until the draft carries the option (the line of the option in decisions-template.yaml says whether an answer of the inputs file writes it or no answer of this build does), a manual alternative frees only the manual step that carries it out, and a refused opt-in to an API resolves to the draft's own path (the steps of the API path are not taken). The draft itself is unchanged by a review in the decisions file. The one exception is an option that declines a default of the draft (choose-the-size, choose-the-snapshot-count, choose-the-zone-per-server, keep-the-source-rules-and-redesign-a-firewall, machine-type-with-a-local-disk, persistent-volume-for-the-data): the run that reads that answer writes its draft without the default, and the value the default stood for is yours to set.
basis: Records group four lists: the open decisions of the TargetPlans of the draft this run wrote, by the family of the producer (security group, routing, identity, logs, server) and the kind of the decision (plan decisions); the open critical semantics of the units, by the contract family and the semantic (critical semantics); the manual actions of the plans, by the family of the producer and the kind of the action (manual actions); and the open statements of the plans about units they write no resource for (a redesign, a review, a block, a failed model, or a step beside a unit whose draft a converter writes), by the family of the producer and the reason (plan statements). Plan decisions and manual actions cover only drafted units whose draft passed StackToIT's own checks, and only the families whose draft this run wrote from a plan: a family with no plan has none to list. A plan statement covers a unit the plan writes nothing for, whether or not a draft check ran over it; a statement that leaves nothing to a person (a unit the plan does not draft and no manual action of it names) is counted (closed_statements) and is no record. A record shows the review of an overlay beside the open state the engine reached; a review closes no critical semantic and changes no draft, target plan, gate, class, confidence or eligibility. An accepted plan decision frees the steps of the execution plan that wait for it only when the answer's effect acknowledges the current draft; an option that changes the draft keeps them held until the draft carries that option (the line of the option in decisions-template.yaml says whether an answer of the inputs file writes it or no answer of this build does). The one exception is an option that declines a default of the draft (choose-the-size, choose-the-snapshot-count, choose-the-zone-per-server, keep-the-source-rules-and-redesign-a-firewall, machine-type-with-a-local-disk, persistent-volume-for-the-data): the run that reads that answer writes its draft without the default, and the value the default stood for is yours to set. Records of the family "convert" are decisions of the converter's own generators, outside every plan: a CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT (a variable whose consumers' STACKIT bounds exclude one another keeps the source default) and an AMBIGUOUS_* selection (the source does not prove which instance, interface, key pair, gateway, peer, subnet, proxy, URL map or health check it means, so the draft holds a required variable without a default); the unit that owns one is not automation-eligible. They are listed for a drafted unit whose plan checks did not fail.

options.title: Export the data from the source and import it with the clients of the target engine
options.effect: A person exports the data from the source and imports it into the STACKIT instance with the clients of its engine during a window the business accepts, then checks that the copy is complete; the clients reach the instance at the host and port its credential states. The source and the target engine may differ (DynamoDB to MongoDB Flex), so the export is converted where they do. The plan holds the steps of this option as typed steps: for a PostgreSQL database, for a MySQL, MariaDB or Aurora MySQL database moving to MariaDB and for an RDS for SQL Server database moving to SQLServer Flex (the native backup, its copy to a STACKIT S3 bucket and the import_database call) the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the dump or backup and the restore or import inside it, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an ElastiCache, MemoryDB or ElastiCache serverless cache moving to a Key Value Store the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy by a client, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster moving to PostgreSQL Flex the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy of the tables by a client (the schema from the catalogs of the cluster, or from pg_dump --schema-only where the preflight shows that it works, and the rows through the PostgreSQL protocol: no AWS page read documents a dump of a cluster), the reconcile and the cleanup; for an OpenSearch store the write freeze, the copy and the reconcile. The decision offers this option only for a store whose STACKIT service documents a way in with such clients: PostgreSQL Flex (for an Aurora DSQL cluster, which has no change stream, this option and the tool of the customer's own are the only ones; the replication of the engine is not offered), MariaDB (the mysql client loads a dump into an empty instance), SQLServer Flex (a .bak file imported with import_database), Key Value Store (the tutorial migrates a Redis instance by the MIGRATE command; for an ElastiCache source, where AWS lists migrate among the commands unavailable for caches running Redis OSS, the copy is a client that iterates the keys with SCAN and copies each with DUMP, PTTL and RESTORE; for a MemoryDB source, where AWS lists migrate, sync, psync, bgsave, save and config among the unavailable commands and the cluster mode is always on, the same client copy runs against every shard primary found with CLUSTER NODES or CLUSTER SLOTS, with TLS where the source has it and an ACL user that reaches every key; whether DUMP, RESTORE and PTTL run on a standard MemoryDB cluster is not stated by AWS, and for a member of a multi-Region cluster, whose page lists PTTL as unsupported, the step says the TTLs are not carried) and OpenSearch (the reindex operation). For a store without a documented way in (MongoDB Flex, a memcached cache) it is not offered and the decision offers the tool of the customer's own alone.

options.title: Replicate the data with the replication of the source engine until the cutover
options.effect: A person sets up the replication of the source engine so that the STACKIT instance follows the source while the application keeps writing to the source (for PostgreSQL, logical replication: the schema is copied first with pg_dump --schema-only, a publication on the source and a subscription on the target copy the existing rows and then the changes, and the sequences are copied inside the write freeze because they are not replicated). The source needs a change and a reboot to turn replication on, and the target must be able to reach the source. Inside the write freeze the person waits until the target has caught up, compares both sides and switches the clients, then removes the replication. For a PostgreSQL database the plan holds the steps of this option (the initial copy, the watch of the lag, the freeze, the final copy, the reconcile and the cleanup); for an S3 bucket this option is not available, because S3 Replication copies between Amazon S3 buckets and no STACKIT bucket is documented as a destination (the plan holds the two copy tools instead); for any other engine this option is not offered, because no STACKIT service other than PostgreSQL Flex documents the replication of a source engine into it (MariaDB, Key Value Store, OpenSearch and MongoDB Flex document none, and the SQLServer Flex page on transactional replication describes an on-premises publisher and does not name Amazon RDS as one), so the decision of such a store offers the export and the import with the engine clients where its service documents them, and the tool of the customer's own.

options.title: Move the data with a migration tool or a replication of the owner's own
options.effect: A person moves the data with a tool or a replication they run (for example a change-data-capture replication that keeps the copy in step until the cutover), writes its steps, the checks before the move, the cutover window and the way back, and carries them out. The STACKIT instance is reached at the host and port its credential states. The plan holds that work as typed steps: the write freeze of the source, the copy as one step whose commands the person writes, and the reconcile that compares both sides; the source stays the way back until the reconcile records GO, which a person checks, since the plan cannot know that the tool leaves the source unchanged. A memcached cache holds a confirmation instead of a copy. A bucket repeated by count or for_each has neither a reconcile nor any other option: its instances and the buckets they move to are not named, so the plan holds the one manual step, which the person writes for each instance after naming them.

effects: A person exports the data from the source and imports it into the STACKIT instance with the clients of its engine during a window the business accepts, then checks that the copy is complete; the clients reach the instance at the host and port its credential states. The source and the target engine may differ (DynamoDB to MongoDB Flex), so the export is converted where they do. The plan holds the steps of this option as typed steps: for a PostgreSQL database, for a MySQL, MariaDB or Aurora MySQL database moving to MariaDB and for an RDS for SQL Server database moving to SQLServer Flex (the native backup, its copy to a STACKIT S3 bucket and the import_database call) the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the dump or backup and the restore or import inside it, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an ElastiCache, MemoryDB or ElastiCache serverless cache moving to a Key Value Store the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy by a client, the reconcile and the cleanup; for an Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster moving to PostgreSQL Flex the preflight, the rehearsal, the write freeze, the copy of the tables by a client (the schema from the catalogs of the cluster, or from pg_dump --schema-only where the preflight shows that it works, and the rows through the PostgreSQL protocol: no AWS page read documents a dump of a cluster), the reconcile and the cleanup; for an OpenSearch store the write freeze, the copy and the reconcile. The decision offers this option only for a store whose STACKIT service documents a way in with such clients: PostgreSQL Flex (for an Aurora DSQL cluster, which has no change stream, this option and the tool of the customer's own are the only ones; the replication of the engine is not offered), MariaDB (the mysql client loads a dump into an empty instance), SQLServer Flex (a .bak file imported with import_database), Key Value Store (the tutorial migrates a Redis instance by the MIGRATE command; for an ElastiCache source, where AWS lists migrate among the commands unavailable for caches running Redis OSS, the copy is a client that iterates the keys with SCAN and copies each with DUMP, PTTL and RESTORE; for a MemoryDB source, where AWS lists migrate, sync, psync, bgsave, save and config among the unavailable commands and the cluster mode is always on, the same client copy runs against every shard primary found with CLUSTER NODES or CLUSTER SLOTS, with TLS where the source has it and an ACL user that reaches every key; whether DUMP, RESTORE and PTTL run on a standard MemoryDB cluster is not stated by AWS, and for a member of a multi-Region cluster, whose page lists PTTL as unsupported, the step says the TTLs are not carried) and OpenSearch (the reindex operation). For a store without a documented way in (MongoDB Flex, a memcached cache) it is not offered and the decision offers the tool of the customer's own alone.

resolution_paths.title: Replicate the data with the replication of the source engine until the cutover
effects: A person sets up the replication of the source engine so that the STACKIT instance follows the source while the application keeps writing to the source (for PostgreSQL, logical replication: the schema is copied first with pg_dump --schema-only, a publication on the source and a subscription on the target copy the existing rows and then the changes, and the sequences are copied inside the write freeze because they are not replicated). The source needs a change and a reboot to turn replication on, and the target must be able to reach the source. Inside the write freeze the person waits until the target has caught up, compares both sides and switches the clients, then removes the replication. For a PostgreSQL database the plan holds the steps of this option (the initial copy, the watch of the lag, the freeze, the final copy, the reconcile and the cleanup); for an S3 bucket this option is not available, because S3 Replication copies between Amazon S3 buckets and no STACKIT bucket is documented as a destination (the plan holds the two copy tools instead); for any other engine this option is not offered, because no STACKIT service other than PostgreSQL Flex documents the replication of a source engine into it (MariaDB, Key Value Store, OpenSearch and MongoDB Flex document none, and the SQLServer Flex page on transactional replication describes an on-premises publisher and does not name Amazon RDS as one), so the decision of such a store offers the export and the import with the engine clients where its service documents them, and the tool of the customer's own.

resolution_paths.title: Move the data with a migration tool or a replication of the owner's own
effects: A person moves the data with a tool or a replication they run (for example a change-data-capture replication that keeps the copy in step until the cutover), writes its steps, the checks before the move, the cutover window and the way back, and carries them out. The STACKIT instance is reached at the host and port its credential states. The plan holds that work as typed steps: the write freeze of the source, the copy as one step whose commands the person writes, and the reconcile that compares both sides; the source stays the way back until the reconcile records GO, which a person checks, since the plan cannot know that the tool leaves the source unchanged. A memcached cache holds a confirmation instead of a copy. A bucket repeated by count or for_each has neither a reconcile nor any other option: its instances and the buckets they move to are not named, so the plan holds the one manual step, which the person writes for each instance after naming them.

options.title: Accept the public endpoint, limited by its access list
options.effect: The endpoint the draft writes is applied as written: the instance (or the Kubernetes API) is reached at its public address, and only the IP networks of its access list may connect (acl of stackit_postgresflex_instance and stackit_sqlserverflex_instance, sgw_acl of stackit_mariadb_instance, extensions.acl.allowed_cidrs of stackit_ske_cluster; parameters.sgw_acl of stackit_valkey_instance (Key Value Store), stackit_opensearch_instance, stackit_rabbitmq_instance and stackit_redis_instance, a comma-separated list of IP networks in CIDR notation, left to the default when the draft states none). The exposure is wider than the source's and the difference is accepted. Maturity: for stackit_ske_cluster this is the ACL-restricted public control plane: GA, not the source's private endpoint (the ACL how-to, last updated Aug 19, 2026, carries no Private Preview or beta notice, and says ACLs only control access to the API of the public control plane); the provider documents acl and sgw_acl of the data services without a preview notice. For an Application Load Balancer: it is created with the access control the draft writes, options.access_control.allowed_source_ranges, one set of source ranges for the whole load balancer (or none, where the draft can prove no range), so it admits more clients than the source's security groups; the restriction the set cannot express is the client-access manual step of the plan behind this decision, which follows the load balancer. The draft carries this option out BY DEFAULT for the Kubernetes API of a cluster whose source endpoint is private (stackit_ske_cluster, extensions.acl): of the three options it is the only one that is production grade (the ACL-restricted public control plane is GA, the network-area-only control plane is a Private Preview on request, not recommended for production, and cannot be combined with the ACL extension) and it is fail-closed, because only the CIDRs of the access list may connect. The decision stays OPEN with this option marked DEFAULT; the access list stays a required variable with no default (no CIDR is invented, and neither the cluster's own egress addresses nor a STACKIT range is a fallback, because the source's private clients are the admin and CI networks only the customer knows) that refuses an empty list, so the step of the cluster waits for the networks the person lists and not for the decision. The draft carries it out by default for a managed data service (stackit_postgresflex_instance, stackit_sqlserverflex_instance, stackit_mariadb_instance, stackit_mongodbflex_instance, stackit_valkey_instance, stackit_opensearch_instance, stackit_rabbitmq_instance, stackit_redis_instance) as well, on the same grounds and only when all of these hold: the decision is open and no review declines it; the access list the block writes (acl, sgw_acl) is one variable the draft wrote, of type list(string), with no default, that refuses an empty list, an empty entry and null; and the draft could not derive the clients' addresses (where every client is a drafted cluster or a drafted server with a public address the access list already has those addresses as its default, and the decision stands on that default). Of the options, accept-the-public-endpoint is the only one that is generally available for every data service (the network-area-only scope is a Private Preview for enabled accounts and exists for PostgreSQL Flex and SQL Server Flex only), and with a required, non-empty list it is fail-closed: only the CIDRs the person lists may connect. No CIDR is invented, and STACKIT's documented service ranges are no fallback. The default applies to a source that is private and to one whose exposure cannot be read, because the draft writes the same fail-closed endpoint for both. The access-scope variable of PostgreSQL Flex and SQL Server Flex keeps no default, and the critical network exposure of the unit stays open for the assurance until a review that chooses this option also states an exposure_acceptance (its statement and scope), which records the public endpoint as an accepted design change naming the reviewer, never as an equivalent. A review that names another option for the record, or rejects the proposal, declines the default. A cluster whose source endpoint is public gets no decision: its public_access_cidrs are the access list.

options.title: Use the network-area-only scope (SNA) instead of the public endpoint (Private Preview, on request)
options.effect: Maturity by target. stackit_ske_cluster: SNA private control plane: Private Preview, on request, not for production, no ACL extension (private preview; the documentation says the feature is available only upon request, is under active development, subject to breaking changes without prior notice, and not recommended for production use, and that a private cluster and the ACL extension are mutually exclusive: the GA way to restrict the Kubernetes API is the ACL-restricted public control plane, which is not the source's private endpoint). stackit_postgresflex_instance and stackit_sqlserverflex_instance: private preview (the provider documents access_scope as a private preview for enabled accounts). stackit_mariadb_instance, stackit_valkey_instance, stackit_opensearch_instance, stackit_rabbitmq_instance, stackit_redis_instance and stackit_application_load_balancer: not offered (no access scope; the redesign option applies). What the option means: The endpoint is reachable only inside a STACKIT Network Area: access_scope = SNA of stackit_postgresflex_instance and stackit_sqlserverflex_instance, network.control_plane.access_scope = SNA of stackit_ske_cluster (immutable). The scope is a private preview, permitted for enabled accounts only (a request of another account is rejected). The draft does not write it, so the source (or the draft) is changed with the scope before the step is applied. The pinned provider documents no access scope for stackit_mariadb_instance: there it is a redesign. Neither does it for stackit_valkey_instance (Key Value Store), stackit_opensearch_instance, stackit_rabbitmq_instance or stackit_redis_instance, whose access is set by parameters.sgw_acl only (the pinned STACKIT provider schema): for a private cache, search domain or broker there is no network-area-only option: the way out is a redesign, so the draft is changed before the step is applied. Neither does it for stackit_application_load_balancer, whose options are access_control, ephemeral_address, observability and private_network_only (accessible only via a private network address, not changeable after creation): there the way out is a redesign (a private load balancer, or the restriction in front of it), so the draft is changed before the step is applied.

options.title: Keep the draft: a NodePort Service of each workload and the target pool on its node port at the private IPs of the cluster's nodes
options.effect: The manifest of each workload writes a Service of type NodePort with the node port the target pool of the drafted Application Load Balancer listens on, and the pool's targets are the private IPs of the nodes of the SKE cluster, which a person sets and keeps current: the nodes change as the node pool scales and is updated, and a node missing from the list receives no traffic. The health check of the pool reaches the pods through the same node port. The targets must be in the same network as the load balancer, and the draft states for each load balancer whether the cluster the workload runs on is deployed into that network. Where it is, nothing more is written. Where it is not shown to be (a cluster that sets no network.id, which SKE places in a network of its own in a project outside a Network Area, a cluster deployed into another network, or a load balancer whose network is not one fixed network of the draft), the targets are treated as outside the network: the draft sets disable_target_security_group_assignment = true on the load balancer, which cannot be changed after creation, and the routing between the two networks and the security group rules that admit the node port from the load balancer to the nodes are a person's work the draft does not generate (whether the two networks can be routed to each other is not shown by the documents read). Setting the IPs is therefore not enough for the draft to apply: the layout of the networks is part of what this option keeps. A Network Load Balancer (stackit_loadbalancer) takes the same path with the same statement and its own attribute, disable_security_group_assignment, which the pinned provider schema describes as primarily used to allow targets that are not within the load balancer's own network or SNA, leaves the connectivity, routing and security group rules to the customer and cannot be changed after the load balancer is created; the documents read for the Network Load Balancer state no same-network rule of their own, so its targets are held to the line of the Application Load Balancer. Only a TCP target group takes the path: a NodePort Service of the draft carries TCP.

options.title: Carry the segmentation as a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that a person writes from the rules of the source group
options.effect: A NetworkPolicy per workload admits the traffic the rules of the source group allowed and nothing else, so the segmentation moves from the interface of the task to the pod. The sources read state that SKE applies NetworkPolicy objects (a default-deny policy of its own in kube-system, and a request to add policies for custom workloads) and give no statement about the policy engine in a workload's namespace, which is checked on the cluster. The draft writes no NetworkPolicy in this build, and the reasons can be shown: a rule that names another security group (the one of the load balancer, for one) names no address or label the draft knows, because the load balancer reaches the pods through a NodePort of the nodes and the cluster exports no node address to Terraform; a policy that leaves out one rule the source admitted blocks traffic the source allowed; and the policy engine of a workload's namespace is checked on the cluster. A person writes the policy from the rules of the drafted group, and the group stays a record of what the source allowed.

evidence.quote: With Kubernetes 1.33 there will be a new deny-all NetworkPolicy introduced, which blocks Network Traffic in the namespace kube-system. If there is custom workload in the namespace, please apply additional NetworkPolicies for Ingress and Egress.
SKE (Gardener) enforces a default-deny `NetworkPolicy` in `kube-system`.

options.title: Carry the segmentation as a STACKIT security group on the nodes (coarser than the source)
options.effect: A security group acts on the network interface that lists it, so on a node and on every pod of it, not on one workload: it is coarser than the source group, which acted on the interface of each task. The provider resource of the cluster has no security group attribute, on the cluster or on a node pool, so the draft cannot write it, and whether the interfaces of the nodes can list a group by another route is not stated by the sources read: a person establishes that with STACKIT before choosing it.

options.title: Keep the plan or machine type the draft derived from the size of the source
options.effect: The draft already writes the derived plan, flavor or machine type (as the default of the variable for a plan or a machine type, as the literal of the block for a database flavor), said as DEFAULT on the block: the instance or the pool is created with it and the cost page prices it. Confirming it accepts the proposal as the starting size of the target; it does not say that the size carries the load, which the source does not state, and the disk of a plan is the smallest of that size. The memory was compared in bytes: the API states the memory of a PostgreSQL Flex and a SQL Server Flex flavor in Gibibyte, the unit of the source; the plan tables of Key Value Store and RabbitMQ and the MongoDB Flex flavors state their RAM as GB without defining it, so the draft took the plan or flavor that holds the source's memory when a GB is 10^9 bytes (it then holds it when a GB is 2^30 bytes as well) and says where that made it larger than the reading of a GB as a GiB; a machine type's memory is the catalogue's ram_mb read as MiB, an inference the API does not state. The next run writes the same default.

The FAQ recommends a cold-storage approach for longer periods: stream the log data in parallel to a long-term storage such as a separate Object Storage bucket. resolution.source_observation: The plan writes no resource for module.vpc.module.vpc.aws_route_table.private: STACKIT's default routing replaces the table, with a loss: a route of the table sends traffic to a NAT gateway (the others, if any, to an internet gateway), and the reachability is observed on the target for a project outside a Network Area, which this draft does not write. Observed in one sandbox project outside a Network Area (tested on a STACKIT project on 2026-10-10; routing tables are refused there): a routed network reaches the internet with no route and no routing table configured, a server without a public IP through the network's shared SNAT address and a server with a public IP through its own; nothing initiated from the internet reached a server behind the network address; egress is restricted by the egress rules of security groups, not by a route; routed networks reach each other with no table. No stackit_routing_table is drafted. A NAT gateway adds what an internet route does not. Its fixed egress address is LOST (observed): the address a routed STACKIT network leaves by is the network's publicIp, one address for every routed network of the project, not fixed (it changed twice when every network of the project was deleted) and not settable (a PATCH of it answers 202 and is ignored), so a third party's allow-list on the NAT gateway's address does not survive; a STACKIT public IP per server keeps its address, the only one the probe saw stay fixed. The egress restriction (the gateway as the only way out of a private subnet) is carried by the egress rules of security groups, not by a route (observed); whether the source restricts egress that way is for the architect. The absence of inbound paths of a private subnet is observed for a server without a public IP (tcp 22, 80 and 8080 on the network address). Not observed: a Network Area and its default routing table. The outbound address of the servers an allow-list names is the architect's choice: keep the changing address, or give each server that an allow-list names a STACKIT public IP. The plan writes no resource for module.vpc.module.vpc.aws_route_table.public: STACKIT's default routing replaces the table: every route of the table sends traffic to an internet gateway, and the equivalence is observed on the target for a project outside a Network Area, which this draft does not write. Observed in one sandbox project outside a Network Area (tested on a STACKIT project on 2026-10-10; routing tables are refused there): a routed network reaches the internet with no route and no routing table configured, a server without a public IP through the network's shared SNAT address and a server with a public IP through its own; nothing initiated from the internet reached a server behind the network address; egress is restricted by the egress rules of security groups, not by a route; routed networks reach each other with no table. No stackit_routing_table is drafted. Observed in one project of one region on one day, so not HIGH; not observed: a Network Area and its default routing table, where this would be open again. The draft writes no routing table for a table whose routes all send traffic to an internet gateway: STACKIT's default routing gave a routed network the same reachability in one STACKIT test project outside a Network Area. The default routing table of a Network Area was never read.

state_definitions.review_state: ARCHITECT_REVIEWED: a review of the decisions file, bound to this run (source digest, knowledge base and members all hold), covers every member of the record and accepts or rejects it; the outcome is the status and the review of the record. UNREVIEWED: none was given, it covers only some members, or its binding no longer holds. A review never closes a plan decision, a critical semantic or a manual action.
state_definitions.design_state: OPEN: this run's plan or draft still carries the item. DESIGN_RESOLVED: stated only for an entry of the decisions file that this run's register does not hold, written for another source digest and the same knowledge base, in a run that read the plans of a generated draft without a degraded reading: the item is gone from the plan or draft of the later source. It is inferred from the absent id, so an id misspelled in the file reads the same way; a review never sets it.
state_definitions.validation_state: TECHNICAL_VALIDATION_PASSED: this run ran tofu validate on the draft, it passed, and the record belongs to a family of the draft (security group, routing, identity or logs) that the validation covered. NOT_VALIDATED: tofu validate was not asked for, did not run, or the record is a critical semantic of the source, which a schema check of the draft does not cover. FAILED: tofu validate rejected the draft that holds the family. It is a static check against the pinned provider schema, not target behaviour and not approval.

options.title: Accept the availability-zone difference of the placement the draft writes for the servers of the subnet
options.effect: The servers the subnet places stay, each with its volumes, in the one Single-AZ zone the regenerated draft writes for them; the STACKIT network of the subnet is regional. A Single-AZ server is not restarted in another zone when its zone fails and its volumes are not mirrored to another zone, so a zone outage takes down what sits in that zone. The Metro zone is no spread either: it restarts a single instance in another zone and may place all instances in one zone. The review accepts that difference with the source zone layout, the target placement of each server, the failure-domain difference, the recovery expectation (RTO and RPO) and the verification it requires; the check then closes as an accepted design change bound to the draft that writes those placements, and frees nothing else.

evidence.quote: In a single AZ setup, a service runs in the specific AZ you select. It won’t be restarted in a different zone if an outage occurs.
Single Availability Zone (Single AZ) setup implies fixed assignment to one Availability Zone. Data in a Single AZ are not mirrored across different Availability Zones.

This failover process can take time but significantly increases uptime for single-instance workloads. For high-availability workloads, Metro AZ behavior is less predictable. Because STACKIT places instances based on system load, all instances may end up in the same AZ.

evidence.quote: With KMS encryption, all secret values in a Secrets Manager instance can be encrypted using a STACKIT Key Management Service (KMS) key. ... Who authorizes? A service account whose email address is stored in the instance’s KMS configuration and which has at least the role “Secrets Manager Reader” or “Secrets Manager Admin” role. ... At the moment it is not possible to configure KMS via the Portal UI.

`kms_key` (Attributes) The STACKIT-KMS key for secret encryption and decryption. ... `key_id` (String) UUID of the key within the STACKIT-KMS to use for the encryption. `key_ring_id` ... `key_version` (Number) ... `service_account_email` (String) Service-Account linked to the Key within the STACKIT-KMS.
Changing keyVersion affects not only new/future write operations. Already stored secrets are automatically re-encrypted.

why_open: Confirm the container definitions of the ECS task definition: The mapping rule for {name} kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes {name} setting to a person; it does not decide its value. ecs_task_definition.container_definitions of the unit that runs the task. The containers of the task: images, commands, environment, secret references, ports, health checks, log configuration - the workload itself, and where its credentials are injected. Decide per container: the image and where it lives, command and entry point, environment, ports and health check, cpu/memory as requests and limits, and the log destination; the secret references and the plaintext secrets among the environment entries are read by the settings of the secret references and of the plaintext secrets, the registry by the setting of the image registry.

Confirm the container image registry: The mapping rule for {name} kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes {name} setting to a person; it does not decide its value. A container image comes from Amazon ECR (a `.dkr.ecr.` or public.ecr.aws registry host) or needs `repositoryCredentials`. The images are not moved by the draft and a pod on STACKIT cannot assume the ECR pull rights of the ECS execution role. Decide: where the images live on STACKIT (the STACKIT Container Registry has a GA API, the Container Registry API specification, but no Terraform resource in pinned provider; a registry of your choice works too), how they are copied, and the pull secret the cluster uses.

Confirm the container plaintext secret env: The mapping rule for {name} kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes {name} setting to a person; it does not decide its value. An `environment` entry whose NAME looks like a credential (password, secret, token, api key, private key, credential) carries a non-empty plaintext value in the task definition (a name heuristic, not a proof: the value is never shown). Decide: whether the value is a secret; if it is, it must not be copied into a Kubernetes manifest or a Terraform variable default but stored in a STACKIT Secrets Manager entry and the plaintext copy in the AWS state and task definition rotated.

Confirm the container secret references: The mapping rule for {name} kind of unit recognises the unit but only passes {name} setting to a person; it does not decide its value. The task definition's container_definitions state secret references (the `secrets` list: name and valueFrom, "the full ARN of the AWS Secrets Manager secret or the full ARN of the parameter in the SSM Parameter Store", AWS ECS API reference, Secret). A person decides first which STACKIT Secrets Manager instance holds each referenced secret (stackit_secretsmanager_instance, pinned provider: name, acls, kms_key; the secret entries themselves have no Terraform resource in the pinned provider, they are created through the API or the portal, and their VALUES are never in the Terraform sources - a person copies them). Second, a person decides how the pods read them (the STACKIT Secrets Manager authenticates with Vault-compatible tokens and AppRole, docs.stackit.cloud/products/security/secrets-manager/; ECS injects valueFrom into environment variables when the container starts, and no STACKIT equivalent of that injection is stated on the documentation page checked 2026-10-06, so the Kubernetes Secret or the in-pod fetch is a design of its own).
